sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Osnabrück's car parks have been getting busier since 2023: 2025 was 6% above 2023, and 2026 so far is 1% above 2025, against a flat German picture. In the same garages, weekday occupancy rose from 36% of spaces in 2022 to 42% in 2025.

The city has used price rather than closures. It says there is no decision to cut on-street parking [0], and it deliberately keeps the street dearer than the garages (twice as dear, in its own words) [1]. Resident permits went from €30.70 a year to €90 in 2023 and €120 in 2025 [3]. OPG's garage prices had last risen in 2013 when a new rise was proposed in 2022 [5]; for 2024 the council approved €2.50 for the first hour and €2.00 for each further hour inside the Wallring [6], and from July 2024 drivers paying by card pay less than the new base rate [7].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
With one public operator, change in Osnabrück is about renovation and payment rather than new entrants. The Kollegienwall garage, one of the busiest in the city, is being renovated in phases until 2028, with parts fully closed in autumn 2026 [11]. New payment terminals since 2024 accept plate entry for lost tickets, with ticketless parking named as the next step [8], and the guidance system that shows free spaces in real time [1] was being moved to new software in October 2026 [12]. OPG runs about 150 charge points, two to three in every garage [10].

The centre lost the Galeria store at Neumarkt in October 2020, and plans to sell the building fell through [13]. In our data the garages more than a kilometre from the town hall grew fastest: from 41% to 53% occupied between 2022 and 2025, against 34% to 38% in the centre.

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
OPG, owned by the city's utility, runs all thirty sites we measure: about 6,700 spaces, a typical price of €1.80 an hour and €18 a day (the tariffs on file look older than the 2024 increase). Without competitors, OPG's pricing is a city policy choice. Within its estate, the dearer garages are also the fuller ones, which suggests OPG charges more where demand is highest rather than using price to steer drivers elsewhere.

The busiest sites are the L&T underground garage by the department store (81% on weekdays), Kollegienwall (75%) and the Bahnhofsgarage (69%), whose prices were cut by up to 30% in 2020 to make it easier to combine car and train [4]. The free park-and-ride at Rubbenbruchsee is almost unused (5%).
